=================== claim--strength-and-speed-training-response-shifts-with-training-age.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "4.1.1"
topic: load selection and training age
category: [strength, programming, training-age]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-27
---

# The Optimal Training Load Percentage, and How to Split Light and Heavy Work, Both Shift With Training Age

**What it is** — Zimkin (1961) reports weightlifter data in which exercises with 45-60% of
1RM were slightly more effective than 60-75% or 75-90% of 1RM loads over the first 8
sessions; after 16 sessions the pattern reversed, with 75-90% of 1RM most effective and
45-60% least effective. Muller & Hettinger (1957) report that novices show a noticeable
strengthening effect using 30-46% of 1RM, while more experienced athletes need at least 60%
of 1RM to keep progressing. Separately, Chernyavsky (1966) ran two groups through 20
sessions using loads of 10% and 40% of 1RM in reversed proportions: the group whose volume
was 80% at 40% of 1RM and 20% at 10% of 1RM gained 44.8% strength and 35.2% movement speed;
the group with the proportions reversed (80% at 10% of 1RM) gained 31.6% strength and 18.3%
speed. (PDF p. 213, printed p. 202.) The same passage repeats, from the same Verkhoshansky
1977 source, the Korobkov/Gerasimov/Vasiliev finding (uniform early strength gains
regardless of load, at 20/40/60/80% of 1RM) already captured in
[[claim--strength-training-threshold-stimulus]] from chapter 1.2; that identical material is
not re-atomized here (see this book's `_book.md` for the dedup note).

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for why the optimal percentage shifts with
training age. Inference: this is consistent with an early neuromuscular-coordination phase
of adaptation that responds to a wide range of submaximal loads (see
[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]), followed by a phase
where further gains require loads closer to the athlete's current ceiling because there is
less slack left in recruitment and coordination to exploit.

**When to apply** — Inference: favor lower relative intensities, and (per Chernyavsky) a
composition weighted toward the heavier of two paired loads, in the first weeks of a new
strength block; shift the emphasis toward higher relative intensity once an athlete has
accumulated meaningfully more exposure (this data uses roughly 16-20 sessions as the shift
point). The Chernyavsky result specifically suggests that when mixing two load zones in one
program, weighting the mix toward the heavier load produced more strength and more speed
than weighting it toward the lighter load, in that particular design.

**When NOT to apply** — These are single old Soviet citations (Zimkin 1961; Muller &
Hettinger 1957; Chernyavsky 1966) with no stated sample size, exercise selection, or modern
replication in this text. Do not treat 44.8%/35.2% or 31.6%/18.3% as precise, transferable
percentages, or 16 sessions as a fixed threshold; use the pattern (early-training load
tolerance is flexible, later-training load selection matters more, and load composition
proportions can change both strength and speed outcomes) directionally.

**Example** — Inference: a novice athlete's first strength block can reasonably use a
simple 45-60% 1RM prescription without losing much compared to a more complex loading
scheme; once that athlete has trained consistently for several months, continuing to
program only in that range would, per this pattern, stop being the most effective choice.

**Related** — [[claim--strength-training-threshold-stimulus]],
[[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]],
[[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]].
=================== claim--delayed-strength-training-effect-lag-before-gains-appear.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "4.1.1"
topic: lag before strength gains appear
category: [strength, adaptation, timing]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-27
---

# Strength Gains From a Training Stimulus Show a Delay Before They Appear

**What it is** — Clarke (1954) is cited for strength continuing to increase for some time
after a course of isometric tension training had already ended. Chernyavsky (1966) is cited
for a marked increase in strength and movement speed from sufficient resistance training
appearing only after at least 20 training sessions. Nyeniskin (1974) is cited for an average
18-25% increase in speed-strength for a controlled movement, observed after a 10-day rest
from intense specialized strength training. The authors write that this last finding "may
be assumed" to connect to "the well-known adaptive inertia of the body and supercompensatory
restoration (adaptive reconstruction) after strength work," offered as a tentative
interpretation, not a stated fact. (PDF p. 213, printed p. 202.)

**Why it works** — The authors themselves hedge the mechanism ("it may be assumed"); no firm
explanation is given. The "adaptive reconstruction" language used here is the same term the
book elsewhere argues is a more accurate replacement for "supercompensation," and which the
book's own single-factor-model critique complicates (see
[[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]]); that separate tension is not
re-argued here.

**When to apply** — Inference: do not judge a new strength stimulus by its first-week
results; per this text, expect delayed emergence of gains across multiple sessions (at least
20, in the Chernyavsky citation), and consider a planned reduced-training or rest period
(10 days, per Nyeniskin) ahead of a competition or a max-effort test if the goal is peak
speed-strength expression on that day.

**When NOT to apply** — Each figure is a single old citation (1954-1974) with no reported
sample size or modern replication in this text. The "at least 20 sessions" figure carries no
stated training frequency, so the real-world duration it implies is unclear; the 10-day
figure comes from one uncontrolled study. Inference: do not treat 18-25% as a precise,
reproducible taper-response number for a current athlete.

**Example** — Inference: an athlete whose new strength-training block shows no visible
change in tested output after two sessions is not necessarily failing to adapt; per this
pattern, testing before roughly 20 sessions have accumulated may understate the true
training effect that is still developing.

**Related** — [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]],
[[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]].
=================== claim--strength-detraining-and-retention-timelines.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "4.1.1"
topic: strength detraining and retention timelines
category: [strength, detraining, recovery, contested]
confidence: contested
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-27
---

# Strength Detrains at Different Rates in Different Studies, and the Book Does Not Reconcile Them

**What it is** — Several old citations describe how strength is lost after training stops,
without being reconciled by the authors. Chistyakov (1965): after 1-2 months without
systematic strength work, skiers' knee extensor strength dropped 5-6% and flexor strength
15-20%, more pronounced in athletes with a higher level of strength development. Muller
(1966): muscles can lose up to 30% of their strength after just one week of total bed rest.
Hettinger & Muller (1955) and Ravick & Larsen (1959): strength loss from complete cessation
of resistance training occurs at approximately the same rate it was gained by training.
Uncited in this passage: even without measurable strength loss, resuming heavy training
after a layoff of as little as 7-10 days can produce pronounced muscle soreness and an
inability to maintain training intensity until recovery. Chernyavsky (1966) tracked the
near-total loss of strength gained from 20 sessions of speed-strength exercise over 5 months
after training ceased: 8.8% lost after month 1, 33.8% after month 2, 60.2% after month 3,
81.5% after month 4, 88.8% after month 5, with the greatest loss between months 2 and 4.
Contradicting that retention picture, Vasiliev (1954) and McMorris & Eklins (1954) report
that strength gained over 40 sessions did not decrease to initial levels even a full year
after training ceased. Khvilon (1974): a significant proportion of the strength gained from
just 10 electrostimulation sessions was maintained for 5 months. DeLorme (1950) and Khvilon
(1974, printed as "Khrolon" in this passage) are cited for strength increases being
maintained longer when accompanied by an increase in muscle mass. (PDF pp. 213-214, printed
pp. 202-203.)

Internal contradiction, recorded rather than resolved: the Chernyavsky data show 88.8% of
the strength gained from a 20-session speed-strength block lost within 5 months, while the
Vasiliev / McMorris & Eklins data show strength from a 40-session block still intact a full
year later. The authors present both without reconciling session count, exercise type
("speed-strength" vs. general strength), or population as the possible explanation.

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given beyond the muscle-mass observation. Inference: the
DeLorme (1950) and Khvilon (1974) finding that gains tied to hypertrophy are retained longer
is consistent with a structural (muscle-mass) component of strength decaying more slowly
than a purely neural (coordination/recruitment) component, which would also be consistent
with why the shorter, speed-strength-focused 20-session block in Chernyavsky's data decayed
faster than the longer 40-session block. The book does not state this explanation itself.

**When to apply** — Inference: for an athlete facing an enforced 1-2 week break (injury,
travel, an in-season bye), expect measurable but partial strength loss (this text's range:
roughly 5-30% depending on tissue and duration) rather than none, and reintroduce intensity
gradually rather than resuming at the pre-layoff working load. For longer layoffs, expect
further loss, but recognize retention may be considerably better when the training block
that produced the gains was longer and likely included a hypertrophy component. **Eric's
baseline:** Applied Performance's stated retraining cadence treats maximal strength as
needing re-exposure roughly every 30 days (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27`). This text's most specific
timelines (5-6%/15-20% loss at 1-2 months; up to 30% after just 1 week of bed rest) are
broadly consistent with treating roughly a month as a meaningful re-exposure window, though
the text itself states no specific re-exposure interval.

**When NOT to apply** — All figures are single old Soviet-era or Western citations
(1950-1974) without stated sample sizes. Bed rest (Muller 1966) is a more severe stimulus
than ordinary detraining and should not be conflated with, for example, an in-season
reduced-volume phase. Do not treat the 5-month Chernyavsky decay curve as applying to all
strength gains; it is specific to a 20-session block of speed-strength exercise, and the
text's own 40-session data contradicts it for longer training blocks.

**Example** — Inference: an athlete returning from a 10-day layoff during an in-season bye
week should be expected to show some soreness and reduced load tolerance on return; per this
pattern, the safer plan is to reintroduce working intensity over several sessions rather than
resuming at the pre-layoff load.

**Related** — [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]],
[[claim--ligament-tendon-adaptation-and-detraining-response]],
[[claim--delayed-strength-training-effect-lag-before-gains-appear]].
=================== framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: framework
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "4.1.2"
topic: training order and combination effects
category: [programming, periodization, sequencing]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-27
---

# Training Is Non-Commutative and Non-Associative: Order and Combination Change the Outcome

**What it is** — The authors borrow two properties from algebra to describe how combinations
of training means, methods and techniques behave. The Commutative Law (A*B = B*A) and the
Associative Law (A*(B*C) = (A*B)*C) are stated to generally NOT hold in sports training.
Training is non-commutative: the order in which exercises or exercise types are performed
changes the outcome. The book's own examples: a squat-then-clean sequence does not give the
same result as clean-then-squat; a distance-running session shortly before a weights session
"will invariably decrease one's strength capabilities." Training is also non-associative:
using means A followed by a complex of means B and C does not give the same result as a
complex of A and B followed by C on its own. The book's own example: a muscle-endurance
regime (A) performed before a complex of plyometrics (B) and Olympic lifting (C) does not
produce the same result as a complex of muscle endurance and plyometrics (A and B together)
followed by Olympic lifting (C) alone. The authors note that with hybrid exercises (several
movements combined into one repetition, cross-referenced to chapter 7.1, not yet ingested in
this pass), the order of the individual movements likewise has a major effect on execution
and effectiveness. (PDF pp. 216-217, printed pp. 205-206.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no physiological mechanism for non-commutativity or
non-associativity as such. They tie it to the general after-effect phenomenon: every
exercise leaves after-effects whose nature, duration and magnitude depend on the intensity,
duration and pattern of loading, and these after-effects can make exercises placed in
different parts of a workout, on different training days, or even weeks apart, interact
positively or negatively. Inference: this is consistent with acute neuromuscular, metabolic
and potentiation carryover from one exercise or session component to the next, which changes
the stimulus actually delivered by whatever comes after it, though the book does not name a
specific physiological carrier for the effect.

**When to apply** — Use this as an argument against judging a training method in isolation
from the order, context and combination in which it is used. The book explicitly calls
blanket statements such as "power cleans are useless," "periodisation doesn't work," or
"circuit training is excellent for general preparation" simplistic and misleading, because
virtually any method can be rendered ineffective or harmful through an inappropriate
combination or timing for a given individual and training stage, while a method that looks
unremarkable in isolation can be effective as part of the right combination and order.

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: the "laws" are a rhetorical borrowing from algebra, not a
tested mathematical model of training; the book gives no quantitative method for predicting
how much a given reordering changes an outcome, only that reordering matters. Do not use
this framework to justify an arbitrarily complex sequencing scheme without evidence that the
specific order chosen actually outperforms the alternative; the framework establishes that
order and combination matter, not which order is best for a given goal.

**Example** — The book's own examples: (1) a squat-then-clean sequence gives a different
result than a clean-then-squat sequence; (2) a distance-running session shortly before a
weights session invariably reduces strength capability; (3) a muscle-endurance regime placed
before a plyometrics-plus-Olympic-lifting complex does not give the same result as
muscle-endurance-plus-plyometrics placed before Olympic lifting alone.

**Related** — [[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]],
[[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]],
[[claim--strength-and-speed-training-response-shifts-with-training-age]] (a related but
distinct effect: that entry's Chernyavsky result is about the proportion of two loads mixed
in a program, not the sequence in which exercises are performed).
=================== framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: framework
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "4.1.2"
topic: training effect taxonomy
category: [programming, adaptation, terminology]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-27
---

# Acute vs. Delayed, and Particular vs. Cumulative: The Book's Taxonomy of Training Effect

**What it is** — The authors distinguish the acute (immediate) training effect (ATE), the
body's short-term improvement or deterioration in functional state right after a strength
means is applied, from the delayed training effect (DTE), the more stable adaptation that
follows once the volume of training influence is sufficient (cross-referenced forward to
chapter 6.7.1, not yet ingested in this pass). Whether the immediate reaction is
deterioration or improvement is said to depend on the exercise's energy cost, which
determines the rest interval needed before the next exercise: the interval can be lengthened
if more rest is needed, or optimally shortened to exploit a beneficial "superimposed
after-effect phenomenon." Separately, the authors distinguish the particular effect (from
one or more unidirectional means, reflecting the specificity of that means and regime) from
the cumulative effect (from a complex of multi-directional means), stating explicitly that
the cumulative effect is not simply the sum of the body's individual functional changes, but
"a complex of new forms of its motor potential" that still contains the specific
characteristics of the particular means used. The authors then state five generalizations
about the training effect of a complex of means: (1) the training effect of any means
diminishes as the athlete's special physical fitness increases; (2) the means used should
produce the optimal training effect relative to the athlete's current functional state; (3)
the after-effect of previous work alters the training effect of subsequent means; (4) the
training effect of a complex of means depends not only on the sum of the individual stimuli
but also on their combination, order of succession and intervals of separation; (5) the
content of special strength training should be a complex of specific stimuli that produces
the strength fitness required for the given sport, matched to the athlete's level of sports
mastery. (PDF pp. 215-216, printed pp. 204-205.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for the ATE/DTE split beyond the energy-cost-driven
rest-interval logic, and the claim that a cumulative effect is "not simply the sum" of
individual effects is stated, not derived. Inference: this is consistent with the general
principle that a training stimulus interacts with the body's current state (fatigue,
potentiation, prior adaptation) rather than acting as an independent, additive input, the
same logic that underlies
[[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]] in the passage immediately
following this one.

**When to apply** — Use the ATE/DTE distinction as a planning lens for ordering exercises
and sessions around desired short-term versus long-term effects: an ATE expected to
potentiate the next exercise justifies a shorter rest interval, while one expected to deplete
justifies a longer one. Use the particular/cumulative distinction to judge whether a training
block's variety is producing an integrated adaptation or just a list of separate,
unintegrated stimuli, and use the five generalizations as a checklist when building a
multi-means training complex.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a conceptual taxonomy, not an operational protocol. The book
gives no specific rest-interval numbers here and no method for judging in real time whether a
given ATE is potentiating or depleting; the fuller treatment is deferred to chapter 6.7.1,
which is pending in this ingest.

**Example** — Inference: pairing a heavy back squat (a depleting ATE) immediately before
max-velocity sprint work would likely blunt that day's sprint quality, while placing the same
squat after the sprint work, or on a separate day, avoids that particular-effect
interference. This illustrates the framework; the book does not give this specific case.

**Related** — [[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]],
[[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]].
=================== heuristic--structured-load-progression-beats-volume-alone-or-random-combination.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: heuristic
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "4.1.2"
topic: volume vs structure in load management
category: [programming, volume, periodization]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-27
---

# A Structured Complex of Means Beats More Volume or a Random Combination of the Same Means

**What it is** — The authors define training load by five characteristics: its resulting
effect (the qualitative and quantitative special work capacity produced), its composition or
contents (the complex of means applied), its structure (the correlation of means), its volume
(the quantity of training work) and its intensity (the difficulty or quality of the work).
They argue that raising training volume alone cannot compensate for a low training effect
from the means being used, but also that there is no guarantee that highly effective,
logically organized specialized means can produce the same special work capacity at a much
smaller volume in less time. Training volume is said to serve two functions: providing a
functional base for further development of special work capacity (called a universal
principle) and raising special fitness primarily through endurance development (said to be
appropriate only for certain sports). The text also states a direct correlation between
training volume and how long a training effect is maintained, and calls volume an important
condition for successful technical preparation. On structure, the authors state that "no one
means or method of special preparation should be considered universal or absolutely
effective"; each means should have its own place in a training stage depending on the sport's
specificity, the athlete's fitness level, prior training loads and the current stage's aims.
Citing Verkhoshansky (1966, 1970), Tatyan (1974) and Khodykin (1975), the authors state that
special strength training using a specific, structured system of different means and methods
produces a significantly greater effect than randomly using the same means and methods
separately, an advantage achieved even at a smaller volume of work. Figure 4.1 (verified
against the page image, PDF p. 214, printed p. 203) depicts this as three curves, "Means A,"
"Means B" and "Means C," each plotting specific training effect against performance and each
saturating at a successively higher ceiling, illustrating that different means have different
effect ceilings and are meant to be introduced in sequence as the athlete's fitness rises.
(PDF pp. 216-217, printed pp. 205-206.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for why a structured, logically-ordered
combination outperforms a random combination at equal or lower volume; the cited studies
(Verkhoshansky 1966, 1970; Tatyan 1974; Khodykin 1975) are not described in this passage
beyond the summary claim. Inference: this is consistent with the non-commutative and
non-associative framing given in the same section
([[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]]): if order and combination
change outcomes, a deliberately structured combination should on average outperform a
randomly-ordered one of equal volume, simply by avoiding combinations that interfere with
each other.

**When to apply** — Inference: when training volume cannot be increased further, whether

training effect.

# The Optimal Training Load Percentage, and How to Split Light and Heavy Work, Both Shift With Training Age

**What it is** — Zimkin (1961) reports weightlifter data in which exercises with 45-60% of
1RM were slightly more effective than 60-75% or 75-90% of 1RM loads over the first 8
sessions; after 16 sessions the pattern reversed, with 75-90% of 1RM most effective and
45-60% least effective. Muller & Hettinger (1957) report that novices show a noticeable
strengthening effect using 30-46% of 1RM, while more experienced athletes need at least 60%
of 1RM to keep progressing. Separately, Chernyavsky (1966) ran two groups through 20
sessions using loads of 10% and 40% of 1RM in reversed proportions: the group whose volume
was 80% at 40% of 1RM and 20% at 10% of 1RM gained 44.8% strength and 35.2% movement speed;
the group with the proportions reversed (80% at 10% of 1RM) gained 31.6% strength and 18.3%
speed. (PDF p. 213, printed p. 202.) The same passage repeats, from the same Verkhoshansky
1977 source, the Korobkov/Gerasimov/Vasiliev finding (uniform early strength gains
regardless of load, at 20/40/60/80% of 1RM) already captured in
[[claim--strength-training-threshold-stimulus]] from chapter 1.2; that identical material is
not re-atomized here (see this book's `_book.md` for the dedup note).

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for why the optimal percentage shifts with
training age. Inference: this is consistent with an early neuromuscular-coordination phase
of adaptation that responds to a wide range of submaximal loads (see
[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]), followed by a phase
where further gains require loads closer to the athlete's current ceiling because there is
less slack left in recruitment and coordination to exploit.

**When to apply** — Inference: favor lower relative intensities, and (per Chernyavsky) a
composition weighted toward the heavier of two paired loads, in the first weeks of a new
strength block; shift the emphasis toward higher relative intensity once an athlete has
accumulated meaningfully more exposure (this data uses roughly 16-20 sessions as the shift
point). The Chernyavsky result specifically suggests that when mixing two load zones in one
program, weighting the mix toward the heavier load produced more strength and more speed
than weighting it toward the lighter load, in that particular design.

**When NOT to apply** — These are single old Soviet citations (Zimkin 1961; Muller &
Hettinger 1957; Chernyavsky 1966) with no stated sample size, exercise selection, or modern
replication in this text. Do not treat 44.8%/35.2% or 31.6%/18.3% as precise, transferable
percentages, or 16 sessions as a fixed threshold; use the pattern (early-training load
tolerance is flexible, later-training load selection matters more, and load composition
proportions can change both strength and speed outcomes) directionally.

**Example** — Inference: a novice athlete's first strength block can reasonably use a
simple 45-60% 1RM prescription without losing much compared to a more complex loading
scheme; once that athlete has trained consistently for several months, continuing to
program only in that range would, per this pattern, stop being the most effective choice.

**Related** — [[claim--strength-training-threshold-stimulus]],
[[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]],
[[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]].

# Strength Gains From a Training Stimulus Show a Delay Before They Appear

**What it is** — Clarke (1954) is cited for strength continuing to increase for some time
after a course of isometric tension training had already ended. Chernyavsky (1966) is cited
for a marked increase in strength and movement speed from sufficient resistance training
appearing only after at least 20 training sessions. Nyeniskin (1974) is cited for an average
18-25% increase in speed-strength for a controlled movement, observed after a 10-day rest
from intense specialized strength training. The authors write that this last finding "may
be assumed" to connect to "the well-known adaptive inertia of the body and supercompensatory
restoration (adaptive reconstruction) after strength work," offered as a tentative
interpretation, not a stated fact. (PDF p. 213, printed p. 202.)

**Why it works** — The authors themselves hedge the mechanism ("it may be assumed"); no firm
explanation is given. The "adaptive reconstruction" language used here is the same term the
book elsewhere argues is a more accurate replacement for "supercompensation," and which the
book's own single-factor-model critique complicates (see
[[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]]); that separate tension is not
re-argued here.

**When to apply** — Inference: do not judge a new strength stimulus by its first-week
results; per this text, expect delayed emergence of gains across multiple sessions (at least
20, in the Chernyavsky citation), and consider a planned reduced-training or rest period
(10 days, per Nyeniskin) ahead of a competition or a max-effort test if the goal is peak
speed-strength expression on that day.

**When NOT to apply** — Each figure is a single old citation (1954-1974) with no reported
sample size or modern replication in this text. The "at least 20 sessions" figure carries no
stated training frequency, so the real-world duration it implies is unclear; the 10-day
figure comes from one uncontrolled study. Inference: do not treat 18-25% as a precise,
reproducible taper-response number for a current athlete.

**Example** — Inference: an athlete whose new strength-training block shows no visible
change in tested output after two sessions is not necessarily failing to adapt; per this
pattern, testing before roughly 20 sessions have accumulated may understate the true
training effect that is still developing.

**Related** — [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]],
[[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]].

# Strength Detrains at Different Rates in Different Studies, and the Book Does Not Reconcile Them

**What it is** — Several old citations describe how strength is lost after training stops,
without being reconciled by the authors. Chistyakov (1965): after 1-2 months without
systematic strength work, skiers' knee extensor strength dropped 5-6% and flexor strength
15-20%, more pronounced in athletes with a higher level of strength development. Muller
(1966): muscles can lose up to 30% of their strength after just one week of total bed rest.
Hettinger & Muller (1955) and Ravick & Larsen (1959): strength loss from complete cessation
of resistance training occurs at approximately the same rate it was gained by training.
Uncited in this passage: even without measurable strength loss, resuming heavy training
after a layoff of as little as 7-10 days can produce pronounced muscle soreness and an
inability to maintain training intensity until recovery. Chernyavsky (1966) tracked the
near-total loss of strength gained from 20 sessions of speed-strength exercise over 5 months
after training ceased: 8.8% lost after month 1, 33.8% after month 2, 60.2% after month 3,
81.5% after month 4, 88.8% after month 5, with the greatest loss between months 2 and 4.
Contradicting that retention picture, Vasiliev (1954) and McMorris & Eklins (1954) report
that strength gained over 40 sessions did not decrease to initial levels even a full year
after training ceased. Khvilon (1974): a significant proportion of the strength gained from
just 10 electrostimulation sessions was maintained for 5 months. DeLorme (1950) and Khvilon
(1974, printed as "Khrolon" in this passage) are cited for strength increases being
maintained longer when accompanied by an increase in muscle mass. (PDF pp. 213-214, printed
pp. 202-203.)

Internal contradiction, recorded rather than resolved: the Chernyavsky data show 88.8% of
the strength gained from a 20-session speed-strength block lost within 5 months, while the
Vasiliev / McMorris & Eklins data show strength from a 40-session block still intact a full
year later. The authors present both without reconciling session count, exercise type
("speed-strength" vs. general strength), or population as the possible explanation.

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given beyond the muscle-mass observation. Inference: the
DeLorme (1950) and Khvilon (1974) finding that gains tied to hypertrophy are retained longer
is consistent with a structural (muscle-mass) component of strength decaying more slowly
than a purely neural (coordination/recruitment) component, which would also be consistent
with why the shorter, speed-strength-focused 20-session block in Chernyavsky's data decayed
faster than the longer 40-session block. The book does not state this explanation itself.

**When to apply** — Inference: for an athlete facing an enforced 1-2 week break (injury,
travel, an in-season bye), expect measurable but partial strength loss (this text's range:
roughly 5-30% depending on tissue and duration) rather than none, and reintroduce intensity
gradually rather than resuming at the pre-layoff working load. For longer layoffs, expect
further loss, but recognize retention may be considerably better when the training block
that produced the gains was longer and likely included a hypertrophy component. **Eric's
baseline:** Applied Performance's stated retraining cadence treats maximal strength as
needing re-exposure roughly every 30 days (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27`). This text's most specific
timelines (5-6%/15-20% loss at 1-2 months; up to 30% after just 1 week of bed rest) are
broadly consistent with treating roughly a month as a meaningful re-exposure window, though
the text itself states no specific re-exposure interval.

**When NOT to apply** — All figures are single old Soviet-era or Western citations
(1950-1974) without stated sample sizes. Bed rest (Muller 1966) is a more severe stimulus
than ordinary detraining and should not be conflated with, for example, an in-season
reduced-volume phase. Do not treat the 5-month Chernyavsky decay curve as applying to all
strength gains; it is specific to a 20-session block of speed-strength exercise, and the
text's own 40-session data contradicts it for longer training blocks.

**Example** — Inference: an athlete returning from a 10-day layoff during an in-season bye
week should be expected to show some soreness and reduced load tolerance on return; per this
pattern, the safer plan is to reintroduce working intensity over several sessions rather than
resuming at the pre-layoff load.

**Related** — [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]],
[[claim--ligament-tendon-adaptation-and-detraining-response]],
[[claim--delayed-strength-training-effect-lag-before-gains-appear]].

# Training Is Non-Commutative and Non-Associative: Order and Combination Change the Outcome

**What it is** — The authors borrow two properties from algebra to describe how combinations
of training means, methods and techniques behave. The Commutative Law (A*B = B*A) and the
Associative Law (A*(B*C) = (A*B)*C) are stated to generally NOT hold in sports training.
Training is non-commutative: the order in which exercises or exercise types are performed
changes the outcome. The book's own examples: a squat-then-clean sequence does not give the
same result as clean-then-squat; a distance-running session shortly before a weights session
"will invariably decrease one's strength capabilities." Training is also non-associative:
using means A followed by a complex of means B and C does not give the same result as a
complex of A and B followed by C on its own. The book's own example: a muscle-endurance
regime (A) performed before a complex of plyometrics (B) and Olympic lifting (C) does not
produce the same result as a complex of muscle endurance and plyometrics (A and B together)
followed by Olympic lifting (C) alone. The authors note that with hybrid exercises (several
movements combined into one repetition, cross-referenced to chapter 7.1, not yet ingested in
this pass), the order of the individual movements likewise has a major effect on execution
and effectiveness. (PDF pp. 216-217, printed pp. 205-206.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no physiological mechanism for non-commutativity or
non-associativity as such. They tie it to the general after-effect phenomenon: every
exercise leaves after-effects whose nature, duration and magnitude depend on the intensity,
duration and pattern of loading, and these after-effects can make exercises placed in
different parts of a workout, on different training days, or even weeks apart, interact
positively or negatively. Inference: this is consistent with acute neuromuscular, metabolic
and potentiation carryover from one exercise or session component to the next, which changes
the stimulus actually delivered by whatever comes after it, though the book does not name a
specific physiological carrier for the effect.

**When to apply** — Use this as an argument against judging a training method in isolation
from the order, context and combination in which it is used. The book explicitly calls
blanket statements such as "power cleans are useless," "periodisation doesn't work," or
"circuit training is excellent for general preparation" simplistic and misleading, because
virtually any method can be rendered ineffective or harmful through an inappropriate
combination or timing for a given individual and training stage, while a method that looks
unremarkable in isolation can be effective as part of the right combination and order.

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: the "laws" are a rhetorical borrowing from algebra, not a
tested mathematical model of training; the book gives no quantitative method for predicting
how much a given reordering changes an outcome, only that reordering matters. Do not use
this framework to justify an arbitrarily complex sequencing scheme without evidence that the
specific order chosen actually outperforms the alternative; the framework establishes that
order and combination matter, not which order is best for a given goal.

**Example** — The book's own examples: (1) a squat-then-clean sequence gives a different
result than a clean-then-squat sequence; (2) a distance-running session shortly before a
weights session invariably reduces strength capability; (3) a muscle-endurance regime placed
before a plyometrics-plus-Olympic-lifting complex does not give the same result as
muscle-endurance-plus-plyometrics placed before Olympic lifting alone.

**Related** — [[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]],
[[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]],
[[claim--strength-and-speed-training-response-shifts-with-training-age]] (a related but
distinct effect: that entry's Chernyavsky result is about the proportion of two loads mixed
in a program, not the sequence in which exercises are performed).

# Acute vs. Delayed, and Particular vs. Cumulative: The Book's Taxonomy of Training Effect

**What it is** — The authors distinguish the acute (immediate) training effect (ATE), the
body's short-term improvement or deterioration in functional state right after a strength
means is applied, from the delayed training effect (DTE), the more stable adaptation that
follows once the volume of training influence is sufficient (cross-referenced forward to
chapter 6.7.1, not yet ingested in this pass). Whether the immediate reaction is
deterioration or improvement is said to depend on the exercise's energy cost, which
determines the rest interval needed before the next exercise: the interval can be lengthened
if more rest is needed, or optimally shortened to exploit a beneficial "superimposed
after-effect phenomenon." Separately, the authors distinguish the particular effect (from
one or more unidirectional means, reflecting the specificity of that means and regime) from
the cumulative effect (from a complex of multi-directional means), stating explicitly that
the cumulative effect is not simply the sum of the body's individual functional changes, but
"a complex of new forms of its motor potential" that still contains the specific
characteristics of the particular means used. The authors then state five generalizations
about the training effect of a complex of means: (1) the training effect of any means
diminishes as the athlete's special physical fitness increases; (2) the means used should
produce the optimal training effect relative to the athlete's current functional state; (3)
the after-effect of previous work alters the training effect of subsequent means; (4) the
training effect of a complex of means depends not only on the sum of the individual stimuli
but also on their combination, order of succession and intervals of separation; (5) the
content of special strength training should be a complex of specific stimuli that produces
the strength fitness required for the given sport, matched to the athlete's level of sports
mastery. (PDF pp. 215-216, printed pp. 204-205.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for the ATE/DTE split beyond the energy-cost-driven
rest-interval logic, and the claim that a cumulative effect is "not simply the sum" of
individual effects is stated, not derived. Inference: this is consistent with the general
principle that a training stimulus interacts with the body's current state (fatigue,
potentiation, prior adaptation) rather than acting as an independent, additive input, the
same logic that underlies
[[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]] in the passage immediately
following this one.

**When to apply** — Use the ATE/DTE distinction as a planning lens for ordering exercises
and sessions around desired short-term versus long-term effects: an ATE expected to
potentiate the next exercise justifies a shorter rest interval, while one expected to deplete
justifies a longer one. Use the particular/cumulative distinction to judge whether a training
block's variety is producing an integrated adaptation or just a list of separate,
unintegrated stimuli, and use the five generalizations as a checklist when building a
multi-means training complex.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a conceptual taxonomy, not an operational protocol. The book
gives no specific rest-interval numbers here and no method for judging in real time whether a
given ATE is potentiating or depleting; the fuller treatment is deferred to chapter 6.7.1,
which is pending in this ingest.

**Example** — Inference: pairing a heavy back squat (a depleting ATE) immediately before
max-velocity sprint work would likely blunt that day's sprint quality, while placing the same
squat after the sprint work, or on a separate day, avoids that particular-effect
interference. This illustrates the framework; the book does not give this specific case.

**Related** — [[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]],
[[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]].

# A Structured Complex of Means Beats More Volume or a Random Combination of the Same Means

**What it is** — The authors define training load by five characteristics: its resulting
effect (the qualitative and quantitative special work capacity produced), its composition or
contents (the complex of means applied), its structure (the correlation of means), its volume
(the quantity of training work) and its intensity (the difficulty or quality of the work).
They argue that raising training volume alone cannot compensate for a low training effect
from the means being used, but also that there is no guarantee that highly effective,
logically organized specialized means can produce the same special work capacity at a much
smaller volume in less time. Training volume is said to serve two functions: providing a
functional base for further development of special work capacity (called a universal
principle) and raising special fitness primarily through endurance development (said to be
appropriate only for certain sports). The text also states a direct correlation between
training volume and how long a training effect is maintained, and calls volume an important
condition for successful technical preparation. On structure, the authors state that "no one
means or method of special preparation should be considered universal or absolutely
effective"; each means should have its own place in a training stage depending on the sport's
specificity, the athlete's fitness level, prior training loads and the current stage's aims.
Citing Verkhoshansky (1966, 1970), Tatyan (1974) and Khodykin (1975), the authors state that
special strength training using a specific, structured system of different means and methods
produces a significantly greater effect than randomly using the same means and methods
separately, an advantage achieved even at a smaller volume of work. Figure 4.1 (verified
against the page image, PDF p. 214, printed p. 203) depicts this as three curves, "Means A,"
"Means B" and "Means C," each plotting specific training effect against performance and each
saturating at a successively higher ceiling, illustrating that different means have different
effect ceilings and are meant to be introduced in sequence as the athlete's fitness rises.
(PDF pp. 216-217, printed pp. 205-206.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for why a structured, logically-ordered
combination outperforms a random combination at equal or lower volume; the cited studies
(Verkhoshansky 1966, 1970; Tatyan 1974; Khodykin 1975) are not described in this passage
beyond the summary claim. Inference: this is consistent with the non-commutative and
non-associative framing given in the same section
([[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]]): if order and combination
change outcomes, a deliberately structured combination should on average outperform a
randomly-ordered one of equal volume, simply by avoiding combinations that interfere with
each other.

**When to apply** — Inference: when training volume cannot be increased further, whether
from time, recovery capacity, or in-season constraints, prioritize reorganizing the
composition, structure and intensity of the training complex over adding more work. Use
Figure 4.1's logic to plan which means (for example, general strength work, then specialized
strength work, then reactive or plyometric work) to introduce as the training effect from the
prior means saturates for that athlete.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a general planning heuristic, not a specific protocol. The
book gives no criteria for identifying, in practice, when a given means has "saturated" for
an individual athlete, and the cited studies are Soviet-era citations not described in enough
detail here to assess their design or effect size.

**Example** — Inference: a program that keeps adding sets of the same exercises indefinitely
to chase more volume, without varying composition or structure as the athlete adapts, is the
failure mode this heuristic warns against. Figure 4.1's "Means A" curve, which saturates
earliest and lowest, represents that means running out of training effect, at which point a
different means ("Means B" or "Means C") is needed to keep raising the athlete's specific
training effect.

**Related** — [[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]],
[[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]].

=========== PDF 212
SUPERTRAINING
THE MEANS OF SPECIAL 
STRENGTH TRAINING
Opinion concerning the means and methods of strength training often repeats itself, with the beginning of the 
modem era identifying more clearly the motor mechanisms of sports technique. This has helped to determine the 
means of strength training more precisely. However, with the improvement in sporting achievements, the effect 
of these means became less marked. The volume of the same exercises was increased, but it was found that this 
approach also has its limitations (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Once again, researchers turned to analysis o f sports 
movements, now equipped with better measuring technology.
This new cycle of research initiated further progress in training methodology. This was the case, for example, 
when information regarding the significance of strength in sport emerged from the laboratory and coaches looked 
optimistically to weight training. The next trend was towards specificity, since studies indicated that the strength 
necessary for the successful execution of one movement has little effect on another movement. Naturally, this 
specificity of strength turned attention to the principle of selectivity in the means of special preparation.
In general, the progress of strength preparation methods leads logically to examination of 
the motor 
mechanisms underlying sports movements. This results in new hypotheses being formulated to replace currently 
accepted ones, beginning with an understanding of actual sports movements and the specific level of the athlete's 
physical fitness. Thus, one can understand why it is necessary to devise new means that cannot easily be rejected 
in favour of fashionable techniques which have become established more on the basis of tradition and emotion 
than on scientific grounds (Verkhoshansky, 1977).
Thus, the selection of the strength and other training means based on the motor specifics o f given sports 
exercises, is one of the most important tasks in sport. This has marked a turning point in training science, which 
has identified the progression of all training from a foundation of general physical preparation (GPP) to 
wbsequent specific physical preparation (SPP), guided by an intimate understanding of the specific character of 
the sports activity. The practice of selecting the means of strength preparation, based upon the specifics of the 
athlete's movements, leads one to abandon reliance on intuition alone and find a more objective foundation.
This foundation is expressed in the form of the principle o f dynamic correspondence, which determines how 
closely the means of special strength preparation corresponds to the functioning of the neuromuscular system in a 
given sport (Vcrkhoshansky, 1977).
4.1 The Problem of Training Means
The process of adaptation involves stimulation from the external or internal environment, which leaves certain 
traces in the body. With repetitive stimulation the traces accumulate, leading to significant modifications which 
raise the functional capability o f the body. A characteristic of every living creature is the relative speed with 
which it adapts to repetitive stimulation. The same regime of stimulation can rapidly produce habituation and 
then fail to elicit any further adaptation, only maintaining the existing levels. Another regime can prove excessive 
and lead to overtraining, which prevents adaptation. An optimum level of stimulation offered in a progressively 
increasing sequence of carefully chosen means is essential for ensuring adaptation at successively higher levels of 
performance (see 1.14).
This, in general and simplified terms, is the physiological foundation of training. In reality it is a very intricate 
process, since systematic exercise as a means of physical conditioning involves a complex of different stimuli 
which affect all systems of the body. 
For example, to successfully increase strength, the load, number of 
repetitions, tempo of execution and workout venue all influence the effectiveness of the training. These variables 
could be listed at great length, since the development of strength is not the only goal o f training. However, 
besides this, it is likely that the coach will select from the vast number of variations, that combination of means 
which he considers will produce the greatest success.
4.1.1 Characteristics of Strength Increase
Strength as a specific result of physical adaptation is determined by the intensity and repetitiveness of the stimuli 
to which the body is exposed during use of the motor apparatus. Only a sufficiently intense level of muscular
201

=========== PDF 213
SUPERTRA/NiNG
contraction, which can be achieved in different ways (e.g. using isometric tension or heavy loads at low velocities), 
will provide an effective training stimulus. Research has shown that the threshold training stimulus necessary for 
increasing muscular strength in the average person should not be less than one-third o f the maximal strength 
(Hettinger & Muller, 1953). As strength increases, the intensity of the stimulus required to produce a training 
effect should be increased, and reach 80-95% of the athlete's maximum. It may be appropriate that the strength of 
the training stimulus sometimes equals or even exceeds the level of the competition stimulus of the given exercise 
(Moroz, 1962; Ratov, 1962; Verkhoshansky, 1963).
Thus, the development of strength requires that the intensity of the stimulus be gradually increased. It was 
discovered that every stimulus has a specific strengthening threshold, the achievement of which fails to elicit any 
further increase in muscular strength (Muller, 1962). The less trained the muscles, the farther the strengthening 
threshold from the initial state. The rate at which strength increases from the initial level to the strengthening 
threshold, expressed as a percentage of the current maximum strength, is independent of sex, age, muscle group 
and the level of the strengthening threshold (Muller, 1962). After the strengthening threshold has been reached 
strength can be increased only by intensifying the training (e.g. by substituting stronger means, devising more 
effective combinations or increasing the volume of work).
These early attempts at establishing general principles need to be more precisely applied in terms of the 
means and methods of strength development, as well as the individual situation. 
For instance, according to 
Korobkov (1953), Gerasimov (1953) and Vasiliev (1954), strength increases relatively uniformly during the initial 
stages of training, independent of how the load is applied in training, whether large or small. Approximately 
equivalent increases in strength arc obtained with loads of 20%, 40%, 60% and 80% of maximum. An increase in 
the intensity o f training in the initial stages (e.g. using a heavier load, faster tempo of movement and shorter 
intervals between sessions) docs not always enhance the effectiveness of strength development, this becoming 
effective only later, as strength fitness increases.
This principle may be illustrated by referring to the training results of weightlifters. Exercises with 45-60% 
of 1 RM in the first 8 sessions are slightly more effective than exercises with 60-75% and 75-90% of 1RM loads. 
After 16 sessions, the most effective load was 75-90% of 1RM, whereas the least effective was 45-60% of 1RM 
(Zimkin, 1961). A noticeable strengthening effect occurs for novices using 30-46% of 1 RM, whereas more 
experienced athletes need to use at least 60% of 1RM (Muller & Hettinger, 1957).
To interpret these factors, one must bear in mind the phasic nature of the response to intense strength loads, 
characterised by a temporary decrease in strength and speed of movement, and the subsequent increase in strength 
and speed after the intensity of the resistance has decreased. Therefore, the effectiveness o f heavy weights does 
not occur immediately, but some time later. It has been shown that strength increases well after sessions of 
isometric tension have ceased (Clarke, 1954), while a marked increase in strength and speed of movement from the 
use of sufficient resistance occurs only after at least 20 training sessions (Chemyavsky, 1966).
An increase averaging 18-25% in speed-strcngth for a controlled movement was noted after a 10 day rest 
from intense specialised strength training (Nyeniskin, 1974). 
It may be assumed that this phenomenon is 
connected with the well-known adaptive inertia of the body and supercompensatory restoration 
(adaptive 
reconstruction) after strength work.
As strength and level of physical fitness increase, dependence of the increase in strength and its effect on the 
type of training becomes more apparent (with reference to the given means and methods). In those cases where 
training is conducted with small loads, there is a concurrent increase in endurance and speed of movement, along 
with the increase in strength, under loaded and unloaded conditions. If large loads are used in training, strength in­
creases significantly, as does the speed of explosive movement. However, endurance under unloaded conditions 
begins to diminish and can even drop below initial levels.
The magnitude o f strength increase and its specific character are also determined by the combination of the 
training means used. For instance, the increase in strength and speed of movement after 20 training sessions in 
which weights of 10% of 1 RM and 40% of 1 RM were used (in different volumes) were as follows: in the group 
whose training volume consisted of 20% with the 10% of I RM load and 80% with the 40% o f 1 RM load, there 
was an increase in strength of 44.8% and an increase of 35.2% in the speed of movement from the initial levels. 
The corresponding figures for the second group doing the reverse combination (20% with 40% of 1RM and 80% 
with 10% of 1 RM) were 31.6% and 18.3% respectively (Chemyavsky, 1966).
The increase in strength also depends upon the athlete's level o f initial strength fitness. In principle, the lower 
the trainee's level o f strength, the greater its increase with training. Virtually all training means prove to be
202

=========== PDF 214
SUPERTRAINING
beneficial in this ease. However, with increase in proficiency, the rate of strength increase diminishes and can be 
elicited only through sufficiently demanding special means of training.
Developing effective methods of strength training involves maintaining the strength already gained. If the 
main goal in the preparatory period is strength development, then it is important that as much strength as 
possible survives into the competition period. In other words, some of the training intensity should be directed at 
preserving the level of strength attained, which is preferable to restoring strength after it has diminished markedly. 
Unfortunately, there are few studies in this area. After 1-2 months without systematic strength work, the 
strength of the extensor muscles decreases by 5-6% and the flexors by 15-20% in skiers. This is especially true 
of athletes who possess a high level of strength development (Chistyakov, 1965). Muscles can lose up to 30% 
of their strength after a period of total (bed) rest of only one week (Muller, 1966). The loss of strength caused by 
complete cessation o f resistance training occurs at approximately the same rate as it is increased by training 
(Hettinger & Muller, 1955; Ravick & Larsen, 1959). Moreover, even if strength level does not decrease, heavy 
strength training after a lay-off from exercise for a period of as little as 7-10 days may result in pronounced 
muscle soreness and an inability to maintain training intensity until full recovery has occurred.
The almost total loss of additional strength which was originally produced by 20 sessions of speed-strength 
exercises was noted 5 months after the special training had ceased (8.8% after the first month, 33.8% after the 
second, 60.2% after the third, 81.5% after the fourth and 88.8% after the fifth month). The greatest loss was 
between the second and fourth months (Chenyavsky, 1966). However, according to other data, strength acquired 
over a period of 40 sessions does not decrease to initial levels even a year after training has ceased (Vasiliev, 1954; 
McMorris & Eklins, 1954). A significant proportion of the increase in strength achieved as a result of ten 
electrostimulation sessions was maintained for 5 months (Khvilon, 1974). It has been noted that an increase in 
strength is maintained fo r a longer period o f time when it is accompanied by an increase in muscle mass 
(DeLorme, 1950; Khrolon, 1974).
Although the above findings give an idea of the general tendencies for the increase and maintenance of 
muscular strength, there are obvious contradictions. Devising reliable methods of special strength preparation 
requires the application of scientific methods to:
• Study the training effect of the means used for a given sport at given levels of fitness
• Determine the optimum sequence, interrelation and continuity of training means for the yearly and multi­
year training periods for different sports and purposes.
Thus, the combination of teaching efforts and special practice should introduce the quantitative programme via the 
basic scheme of special strength training depicted in Figure 4.1, where A, B and C are training means of 
successively greater training effect for a given athlete. In this respect, it should be noted that:
• The contribution of different training means to developing the key motor abilities diminishes with 
improvement in athletic results
• These means are different in terms of their training effect and the use of each of them is justified only when 
the athlete's level of fitness is taken into consideration.
In other words, with growth in sporting proficiency, it is necessary to determine the sequence for introducing the 
chosen means into the training process by calculating the growth and continuity of their training effect. This 
forms the basis for the progressive increase in special work capacity.
Figure 4.1 The introduction of different means with higher training effect (Verkhoshansky, 1977).
203

=========== PDF 215
SUPERTRAININC
4.1 .2  The Effect of the Strength Training Means
In recent years scientific research and years of practical experience have yielded a wealth of findings on whka 
current methods o f special strength training are based. However, it is necessary to note that this material s I 
generalised and its analysis is theoretical. Although today's athletes attain a high level of sport proficiency, then I 
is still no basis to state that this is the result of a precise methodology of special strength training. To a grot 
extent they achieve proficiency through a large volume of strength work and a colossal expenditure of energy. 
Generally, the selection and use of means for organising special strength training has a number of weaknesses.
Despite its apparent diversity, the range of special strength training means is rather limited. In effect 
beginners and highly qualified athletes use essentially the same means, the difference being largely in the volume 
and intensity of their loads.
Firstly, this leads to training monotony and secondly, the body adapts to a repeated stimulus and doeswx 
respond with the desired level of adaptation. Qualified athletes therefore spend much time using ineffective 
means, none of which improves their level of strength fitness. Beginners, on the other hand, often use vigorous ' 
overloading methods for which they are not yet prepared and disrupt the natural process o f achieving spon 
mastery.
An essential shortcoming in the organisation o f strength training is that athletes pay little attention to the 
phenomenon of the qualitative specificity of the training effect of strength exercises. Therefore, very often they 
use means whose specific training effect relates only weakly to the demands placed upon the body by the 
fundamental exercises. For instance, exercises that are selected for strength development often offer only general 
conditioning.
At the other extreme, there is the attempt to select exercises which are structurally similar to the fundamental 
exercises. This may be justified under certain circumstances, but it is sometimes carried to absurd lengths and 
athletes devise such intricate exercises that they are even less effective than traditional general conditioning 
movements. 
This reveals that any system o f special training is deficient if it arbitrarily combines general 
developmental and special strength exercises.
In order to devise a sound scientific system it is necessary to evaluate objectively the training effect of the 
strength means. The training effect is result of the influence of a means or complex of means on the body as 
revealed by the magnitude, quality and stability of the resulting adaptive changes. A number of specific factors 
which reflect the training effect are examined for selecting the training means and devising a methodical system of 
special strength preparation.
It is first of all necessary to distinguish (see 6.7.1) between the acute (immediate) training effect (ATE) and 
the delayed training effect (DTE). The body's immediate reaction to the application of a strength means is 
expressed in a short-term improvement of or deterioration in the athlete's current functional state. Deterioration 
or improvement depends upon the energy cost of the task, which determines the rest interval prior to execution of 
the next exercise: it may be increased if the body requires more rest or be optimally shortened if the superimposed 
after-effect phenomenon is exploited beneficially by the body. The negative reaction of the body is thus removed, 
as revealed by its relatively stable adaptation, which is substantial only if the volume of the training influence is 
sufficient.
The particular effect and cumulative effect are the result of the use of one or more unidirectional means or a 
complex of multi-directional means. In the first case, the adaptation reflects the specificity of the means used in 
the given regime. In the second case, the adaptation displays an integrated, generalised character. However, this is 
not simply the sum of the body's functional changes, but a complex of new forms of its motor potential which 
contains the specific characteristics of the particular training means.
The athlete's success depends largely upon the skill to select a diverse spectrum of exercise means which will 
produce the required cumulative training effect. 
One should also take into consideration factors that are 
characteristic of the training effect, such as absolute and relative strength, muscular endurance, stability and 
temporal features. It is necessary to evaluate the effectiveness of two or more means in order to select the one 
which produces the optimal increase in absolute strength. The qualitative and quantitative characteristics of the 
training effect provide measures of its specific form and the magnitude of improvement in performance. Finally, 
the stability and temporal characteristics of the training effect are evaluated by the length of time for which it is 
maintained.
204

=========== PDF 216
SUPERTRAINING
An examination of the specific factors and the characteristics of the training effect of the strength means 
underlines the complexity of planning the strength training. Although the basis for selecting a strength means by 
taking into account these indicators and their characteristics is convincing, it still offers a very limited foundation, 
so the probability that the athlete will attain the desired level of strength preparation is slight.
To eliminate this problem, it is necessary, firstly, to pay serious attention to objectively evaluate the training 
effect of the strength exercises currently used, and secondly, to conduct scientific research aimed at formulating 
theoretical and practical solutions to optimise the cumulative effect of a complex of strength means. In this 
regard, very little has been done, although some generalisations may be made:
1. The training effect of any means diminishes as one's special physical fitness increases
2. The means used should produce the optimal training effect relative to the one's current functional state
3. The after-effect of previous work alters the training effect of any subsequent methods
4. The training effect of a complex of means is determined not only by the sum of the stimuli, but also their
combination, order of succession and intervals of separation
5. The content of special strength training should include a complex of specific stimuli and produce the
strength fitness required for the given sport, based upon the athlete's level of sports mastery.
With respect to 4 above, application of some mathematical concepts may be useful, as shown below.
Algebraic R elations and Training
Two algebraic laws may be applied to the interaction between different means, methods and techniques in 
strength (and all sports) training , which are important because they are not generally obeyed in training:
• The Commutative Law 
A*B = B*A
• The Associative Law 
A*(B*C) = (A*B)*C
A system may be said to be commutative if it does not matter in which order the operations arc done in that 
system, i.e. A*B * B*A, where * is some special operation. In sports training, this is not the case, sincc the 
order in which one carries out exercises or kinds of exercises can change the outcome, as pointed out in point 3 
ibove. For example, consider a squat and clean sequence: Clean*Squat * Squat*Clean. Thus, sports training 
means may be classed as non-commutative. For instance, a distance running session shortly before a weights 
session will invariably decrease one’s strength capabilities.
Similarly, over the longer term of successive microcycles or mesocycles in a periodised program, the after­
effect phenomenon decrees that the outcome is affcctcd by the order of training means. In the various methods of 
complex training (combinations of different means in individual sessions or longer cycles), the order of the 
components of a complex determine the outcome and effectiveness of the system. With hybrid exercises (Ch 7.1), 
which comprise several movements in one repetition, the order of the individual movements also has a major 
effect on the execution and effectiveness of the exercise.
The Associative Law is also relevant. A system is said to be associative if the operations follow this law: 
A*(B*C)« (A*B)*C. Sports training is non-associative, since the use of means A followed by a complex of two 
means, B and C does not yield the same result as a complex of means A and B, followed by the use of a single 
means C. Thus, the use of a muscle endurance regime A before a complex of plyometrics B and Olympic lifting C 
does not yield the same results as the use of a complex of muscle endurance A and plyometrics B, followed by 
Olympic lifting C on its own.
The non-commutative and non-associative nature o f sports training is central to its overall prescription, 
organisation and management, and should be recalled whenever there is any temptation to design training 
programmes or periodisation schemes solely on the basis of individual exercises, techniques, volumes, intensities 
and  phases. Every exercise is followed by after-effects, the nature, duration and magnitude of these depending on 
factors such as intensity, duration and pattern of loading, and these after-effects deem that exercises in different 
ports of a workout, on different training days and even separated by several days or weeks can interact positively 
or negatively.
Therefore, it is vital that the contcxt of any training situation in space and time be considered when drawing 
up a training programme. Remarks such as “plyometric training is dangerous”, “power cleans are useless”, 
"periodisation doesn’t work”, “weight training is contraindicated for endurance athletes” and “circuit training is
205

=========== PDF 217
SUPERTRAINING
excellent for general preparation” may then be seen to be simplistic and misleading. Virtually any training 
may be rendered impotent or harmful if it is administered in an inappropriate manner for a given individual 
given stage of his/her training career. 
Conversely, methods which may appear to be offer only mz 
improvements on their own, may in optimal combinations yield results which clearly show that “the whole 
greater than the sum of its parts”.
Steps Towards Structuring the Training Process
One issue is still very important for devising methods of strength training. A training effect occurs through 
frequent and systematic repetition of a complex of different interacting means. The training load is understood 
be the sum of all the specific influences on the body, its essential characteristics being:
• its resulting effect (the qualitative and quantitative assessment of the special work capacity of the athlete)
• its composition or contents (the complex of means applied)
• its structure (correlation of means)
• its volume (the quantity of the training work)
• its intensity (the difficulty or quality of the training work).
To assess the effectiveness o f the training process, it is appropriate to examine further how the composi 
structure, the volume and intensity of the training load relate to the resulting effect. The purpose of managing 
training load is to obtain a pronounced and safe training effect through the logical organisation of the com 
and structure of the load, by use of an optimal volume and intensity of exercise.
A load will prove effective if its means create an adequate training effect, i.e. evoke specific adaptation in 
body. This is especially important for highly qualified athletes, since the means they have used in previous staga

modem era identifying more clearly the motor mechanisms of sports technique. This has helped to determine the

This new cycle of research initiated further progress in training methodology. This was the case, for example,

necessary for the successful execution of one movement has little effect on another movement. Naturally, this 
specificity of strength turned attention to the principle of selectivity in the means of special preparation.
In general, the progress of strength preparation methods leads logically to examination of 
the motor 
mechanisms underlying sports movements. This results in new hypotheses being formulated to replace currently 
accepted ones, beginning with an understanding of actual sports movements and the specific level of the athlete's 
physical fitness. Thus, one can understand why it is necessary to devise new means that cannot easily be rejected 
in favour of fashionable techniques which have become established more on the basis of tradition and emotion 
than on scientific grounds (Verkhoshansky, 1977).
Thus, the selection of the strength and other training means based on the motor specifics o f given sports 
exercises, is one of the most important tasks in sport. This has marked a turning point in training science, which 
has identified the progression of all training from a foundation of general physical preparation (GPP) to 
wbsequent specific physical preparation (SPP), guided by an intimate understanding of the specific character of 
the sports activity. The practice of selecting the means of strength preparation, based upon the specifics of the 
athlete's movements, leads one to abandon reliance on intuition alone and find a more objective foundation.
This foundation is expressed in the form of the principle o f dynamic correspondence, which determines how 
closely the means of special strength preparation corresponds to the functioning of the neuromuscular system in a 
given sport (Vcrkhoshansky, 1977).
4.1 The Problem of Training Means
The process of adaptation involves stimulation from the external or internal environment, which leaves certain 
traces in the body. With repetitive stimulation the traces accumulate, leading to significant modifications which 
raise the functional capability o f the body. A characteristic of every living creature is the relative speed with 
which it adapts to repetitive stimulation. The same regime of stimulation can rapidly produce habituation and 
then fail to elicit any further adaptation, only maintaining the existing levels. Another regime can prove excessive 
and lead to overtraining, which prevents adaptation. An optimum level of stimulation offered in a progressively 
increasing sequence of carefully chosen means is essential for ensuring adaptation at successively higher levels of 
performance (see 1.14).
This, in general and simplified terms, is the physiological foundation of training. In reality it is a very intricate 
process, since systematic exercise as a means of physical conditioning involves a complex of different stimuli 
which affect all systems of the body. 
For example, to successfully increase strength, the load, number of 
repetitions, tempo of execution and workout venue all influence the effectiveness of the training. These variables 
could be listed at great length, since the development of strength is not the only goal o f training. However, 
besides this, it is likely that the coach will select from the vast number of variations, that combination of means 
which he considers will produce the greatest success.
4.1.1 Characteristics of Strength Increase
Strength as a specific result of physical adaptation is determined by the intensity and repetitiveness of the stimuli 
to which the body is exposed during use of the motor apparatus. Only a sufficiently intense level of muscular

will provide an effective training stimulus. Research has shown that the threshold training stimulus necessary for 
increasing muscular strength in the average person should not be less than one-third o f the maximal strength 
(Hettinger & Muller, 1953). As strength increases, the intensity of the stimulus required to produce a training 
effect should be increased, and reach 80-95% of the athlete's maximum. It may be appropriate that the strength of 
the training stimulus sometimes equals or even exceeds the level of the competition stimulus of the given exercise 
(Moroz, 1962; Ratov, 1962; Verkhoshansky, 1963).
Thus, the development of strength requires that the intensity of the stimulus be gradually increased. It was 
discovered that every stimulus has a specific strengthening threshold, the achievement of which fails to elicit any 
further increase in muscular strength (Muller, 1962). The less trained the muscles, the farther the strengthening 
threshold from the initial state. The rate at which strength increases from the initial level to the strengthening 
threshold, expressed as a percentage of the current maximum strength, is independent of sex, age, muscle group 
and the level of the strengthening threshold (Muller, 1962). After the strengthening threshold has been reached 
strength can be increased only by intensifying the training (e.g. by substituting stronger means, devising more 
effective combinations or increasing the volume of work).
