means and methods of strength development, as well as the individual situation. 
For instance, according to 
Korobkov (1953), Gerasimov (1953) and Vasiliev (1954), strength increases relatively uniformly during the initial 
stages of training, independent of how the load is applied in training, whether large or small. Approximately 
equivalent increases in strength arc obtained with loads of 20%, 40%, 60% and 80% of maximum. An increase in 
the intensity o f training in the initial stages (e.g. using a heavier load, faster tempo of movement and shorter 
intervals between sessions) docs not always enhance the effectiveness of strength development, this becoming 
effective only later, as strength fitness increases.

of 1 RM in the first 8 sessions are slightly more effective than exercises with 60-75% and 75-90% of 1RM loads. 
After 16 sessions, the most effective load was 75-90% of 1RM, whereas the least effective was 45-60% of 1RM 
(Zimkin, 1961). A noticeable strengthening effect occurs for novices using 30-46% of 1 RM, whereas more 
experienced athletes need to use at least 60% of 1RM (Muller & Hettinger, 1957).
To interpret these factors, one must bear in mind the phasic nature of the response to intense strength loads, 
characterised by a temporary decrease in strength and speed of movement, and the subsequent increase in strength 
and speed after the intensity of the resistance has decreased. Therefore, the effectiveness o f heavy weights does 
not occur immediately, but some time later. It has been shown that strength increases well after sessions of 
isometric tension have ceased (Clarke, 1954), while a marked increase in strength and speed of movement from the 
use of sufficient resistance occurs only after at least 20 training sessions (Chemyavsky, 1966).
An increase averaging 18-25% in speed-strcngth for a controlled movement was noted after a 10 day rest 
from intense specialised strength training (Nyeniskin, 1974). 
It may be assumed that this phenomenon is 
connected with the well-known adaptive inertia of the body and supercompensatory restoration 
(adaptive 
reconstruction) after strength work.
As strength and level of physical fitness increase, dependence of the increase in strength and its effect on the 
type of training becomes more apparent (with reference to the given means and methods). In those cases where 
training is conducted with small loads, there is a concurrent increase in endurance and speed of movement, along 
with the increase in strength, under loaded and unloaded conditions. If large loads are used in training, strength in­
creases significantly, as does the speed of explosive movement. However, endurance under unloaded conditions 
begins to diminish and can even drop below initial levels.

training means used. For instance, the increase in strength and speed of movement after 20 training sessions in 
which weights of 10% of 1 RM and 40% of 1 RM were used (in different volumes) were as follows: in the group

was an increase in strength of 44.8% and an increase of 35.2% in the speed of movement from the initial levels.

the trainee's level o f strength, the greater its increase with training. Virtually all training means prove to be

beginners and highly qualified athletes use essentially the same means, the difference being largely in the volume

phenomenon of the qualitative specificity of the training effect of strength exercises. Therefore, very often they 
use means whose specific training effect relates only weakly to the demands placed upon the body by the 
fundamental exercises. For instance, exercises that are selected for strength development often offer only general 
conditioning.

exercises. This may be justified under certain circumstances, but it is sometimes carried to absurd lengths and 
athletes devise such intricate exercises that they are even less effective than traditional general conditioning 
movements.

developmental and special strength exercises.

strength means. The training effect is result of the influence of a means or complex of means on the body as 
revealed by the magnitude, quality and stability of the resulting adaptive changes. A number of specific factors 
which reflect the training effect are examined for selecting the training means and devising a methodical system of 
special strength preparation.

the delayed training effect (DTE). The body's immediate reaction to the application of a strength means is 
expressed in a short-term improvement of or deterioration in the athlete's current functional state. Deterioration 
or improvement depends upon the energy cost of the task, which determines the rest interval prior to execution of

after-effect phenomenon is exploited beneficially by the body. The negative reaction of the body is thus removed, 
as revealed by its relatively stable adaptation, which is substantial only if the volume of the training influence is 
sufficient.

complex of multi-directional means. In the first case, the adaptation reflects the specificity of the means used in 
the given regime. In the second case, the adaptation displays an integrated, generalised character. However, this is 
not simply the sum of the body's functional changes, but a complex of new forms of its motor potential which 
contains the specific characteristics of the particular training means.

produce the required cumulative training effect.

characteristic of the training effect, such as absolute and relative strength, muscular endurance, stability and 
temporal features. It is necessary to evaluate the effectiveness of two or more means in order to select the one

training effect provide measures of its specific form and the magnitude of improvement in performance. Finally, 
the stability and temporal characteristics of the training effect are evaluated by the length of time for which it is 
maintained.

---
type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "2.3.1"
topic: transfer of physical qualities with rising fitness
category: [transfer, specificity, general-preparation]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# Transfer Between Physical Qualities (Strength, Speed, Endurance) Shrinks as an Athlete's Specific Fitness Rises

**What it is** — Summarizing a body of Soviet and Western literature (Zimkin 1956/1965;
Zatsiorsky 1961/1965; Yakovlev et al 1960; Hebb 1949; Lindeburg 1949; Nelson 1957; Woodworth
1958; Cratty 1964, 1968; Cumbeca et al 1957; Bachman 1961; Lawther 1968; Barrow 1971;
Korobkov 1958), the authors report several established findings on how general physical
qualities (strength, speed, endurance) relate to each other over an athlete's development:
transference of physical qualities decreases as specific fitness increases; the transfer
mechanism is largely specific rather than general; the relationship between physical
qualities can be positive, negative, or neutral; and positive transfer between qualities in
early training can turn into negative transfer later (Korobkov, 1958). They also note it was
often claimed that complex training combining speed, strength, and endurance work develops
each quality better than training each individually (Ozolin, 1949, 1970), but state this
specific claim's validity is examined later in the book rather than settled here. The
following paragraph states a related but separate point, in tension with the above: "the
development of each quality positively influences the development of the others," and a lag
in developing one or more qualities "limits the development of the others" (Krestovnikov
1951; Kaledin 1961; printed 116). This is about qualities supporting each other's
development, not about transfer shrinking as specific fitness rises; the text does not
reconcile the two points, and this entry records both rather than picking one. (PDF pp.
127-128, printed pp. 116-117.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for why transfer specifically *decreases*
as specific fitness increases. The conditioned-reflex model of learned muscular activity is
given for the adjacent point above (why qualities support each other's development), not
for the transfer-decrease finding: training builds an extensive background of "temporary
connections" that different combinations of motor activity can later draw on; the text
states, as a training prescription rather than an observed fact, that "the training means
should develop the motor qualities separately" before combined work (printed 116).
**Inference:** the transfer-decrease finding itself is functionally consistent with the more
detailed ten-dimension specificity principle from Chapter 1 (see
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]]), applied here at the coarser level of
whole physical qualities (strength/speed/endurance) rather than the ten specific training
dimensions within strength itself; this link is not stated in the text.

**When to apply** — Use this as the rationale for reducing reliance on general physical
qualities (e.g. general conditioning, general strength) as an athlete advances, and shifting
training emphasis toward sport-specific expressions of those qualities as specific fitness
rises. **Eric's baseline:** the department already sequences training from general
preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises
(Bondarchuk) rather than treating "sport specific" as a single category
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`, `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`). **Inference:**
this claim supports that same general-to-specific sequencing logic, and adds the caution that
positive transfer seen in an athlete's early training years should not be assumed to persist
unchanged as that athlete advances; a quality that helped early on can plateau in usefulness,
or even work against continued improvement, later.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the "complex training" question (whether training
speed, strength, and endurance together beats training them separately) is explicitly left
unresolved in this passage; do not cite this section as evidence for or against combined
training methods, since the authors themselves defer that judgment to later chapters not yet
ingested. This claim is also a summary of an older, mixed literature base spanning several
decades and traditions (1920s-1970s, per the cited list, printed 116-117), not a single controlled study; treat the general
direction (transfer shrinks with rising specificity) as the useful takeaway rather than any
precise magnitude. The authors themselves add a caution one page later: much of the
specificity literature draws on subjects of low sports qualification, sports mastery is not
accounted for, and conclusions "should be very cautious" and not generalized beyond the
athletes they were drawn from (printed 117).

**Example** — **Inference:** a young multi-sport high-school athlete's general strength and
conditioning work is likely to transfer broadly across several sports; the same general
strength and conditioning work in a veteran college athlete already near the ceiling of his
sport-specific qualities is expected, per this claim, to transfer far less, and may need to
be replaced by increasingly sport- and position-specific training to keep producing gains.
This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Chapter 1),
[[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]],
[[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]] (Chapter 1);
[[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]]
(Bondarchuk's positive/negative/neutral transfer taxonomy, a compatible framing of the same
general topic).

type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "1.2"
topic: minimum effective training load
category: [strength, programming, training-age]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-26
---

# A Minimum Load Threshold Drives Strength Gains, and It Rises as the Athlete Adapts

**What it is** — Hettinger & Muller (1953) are cited for a threshold training stimulus of
roughly one-third of maximal strength needed to produce a strength increase in an average
person; as strength rises, the required stimulus intensity rises too, eventually reaching
80-95% of the athlete's maximum, sometimes matching or exceeding actual competition
intensity (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Each stimulus level has its own "strengthening
threshold," a ceiling beyond which no further gain occurs at that intensity, and this
ceiling is described as further from the untrained state the less trained the athlete is.
Separately, Korobkov, Gerasimov & Vasiliev (via Verkhoshansky, 1977) are cited for the
finding that in the initial stages of training, strength increases roughly uniformly
regardless of load, with approximately equivalent gains reported at 20%, 40%, 60% and 80%
of 1RM; raising training intensity early (heavier load, faster tempo, shorter intervals
between sessions) does not reliably improve on this until strength has already progressed
some way. (PDF pp. 33-34, printed pp. 22-23.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism. Inference: early neuromuscular
adaptation (see
[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]) responds to almost
any sufficiently repeated stimulus above a low floor; once that easy adaptive window
closes, further progress requires a stimulus that approaches the athlete's current
ceiling, because there is less slack left in recruitment and coordination to exploit.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** supports keeping early-phase (novice) load prescription
simple and consistency-focused rather than chasing high intensities, and supports
progressively raising relative intensity toward 80-95% of max as an athlete's training age
increases, consistent with this book's own training-age-scaling heuristic
([[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]]).

**When NOT to apply** — These are single-source, decades-old figures cited without a
stated sample or modern replication in this text (Hettinger 1961; Korobkov, Gerasimov &
Vasiliev via Verkhoshansky 1977; PDF pp. 33-34, printed pp. 22-23). **Inference:** do not
treat "one-third of max" or the specific 20/40/60/80% equivalence as precise, universal
cutoffs for a current athlete population; use them as a directional argument for why novice
programming can be simple, not as exact percentages to program from.

**Example** — **Inference:** A true beginner's program built around consistent submaximal loading (e.g.
50-60% 1RM) can produce comparable early strength gains to a heavier protocol, so there is
little value in front-loading high intensity before the athlete has trained long enough to
need it.

**Related** — [[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]],
[[periodization--bompa/principle--progressive-overload-threshold]].

# Residual Training Effects Last Different Numbers of Days for Different Motor Abilities

**What it is** — The residual training effect is defined as "the retention of changes
induced by systematic workloads beyond a certain time period after the cessation of
training," a term Issurin attributes to Brian and James Counsilman (1991) (PDF p. 33,
printed p. 22). Issurin & Lustig (2004) is cited as the source of Table 1.6 (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), giving residual duration ± SD in days after cessation of training for each
motor ability: **aerobic endurance 30 ± 5 days**, **maximum strength 30 ± 5 days**,
**anaerobic glycolytic endurance 18 ± 4 days**, **strength endurance 15 ± 5 days**,
**maximum speed (alactic) 5 ± 3 days**. Table 1.6's own physiological-background column
lists aerobic endurance's residual as resting on increased aerobic enzymes, mitochondria,
muscle capillaries, hemoglobin capacity, glycogen storage, and fat-metabolism rate, and
maximum strength's on improved neural mechanism and muscle hypertrophy from fiber
enlargement, with no percentages attached in the table itself. Later in the text (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), Issurin gives a specific figure for one of those table items: aerobic
enzymes increase by 40-90% with training (Volkov, 1986; Fox et al., 1993; Wilmore & Costill,
1993). He contrasts this with much smaller local adaptations from sprint training:
phosphocreatine storage (+2-5%), peak lactate accumulation (+10-20%), and anaerobic enzymes
(+2-20%), given without a citation on that page. On the following page (PDF p. 36, printed
p. 25), Thorstensson (1988) is cited specifically for "relatively small increases" in
quickly available energy sources, ATP and phosphocreatine, and enzymes such as creatine
kinase, from highly concentrated sprint training.

**Why it works** — Issurin states the mechanism directly (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp. 24-25):
aerobic ability, supported by pronounced morphological and biochemical changes, is retained
"for a number of weeks at near-peak level," while anaerobic abilities, particularly maximum
sprint speed, "retain near-peak levels for much shorter periods" because peak speed's gains
are smaller and rest on "very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions, which
are relatively unstable and cannot be maintained at the highest level without specially
organized training." Maximum strength's comparably long residual is attributed to pronounced
morphological, biochemical, and neural changes: enlargement of muscle-fiber cross-sectional
area, hyperplasia, recruitment of previously inactive motor units, synchronization of their
activity, and increased motor-neuron discharge frequency (Zatsiorsky, 1995). Strength
endurance's residual is stated to depend on event duration and the degree of
anaerobic-resource mobilization; longer-duration strength endurance has a relatively longer
residual thanks to aerobic adaptation.

**When to apply** — Sequencing which ability to develop first in a training stage (see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]). **Inference:** an ability
with a long residual (aerobic endurance, max strength, 30 ± 5 d) can be built early and
carried further without direct work than a short-residual one, but a stage longer than about
30 days after accumulation ends needs a retention dose (see Example); max speed (5 ± 3 d)
needs re-exposure close to competition. **Eric's baseline directly echoes half of this table:** "Training
residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need
re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue
readiness for max-velocity work degrades" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` p.27). This 30/30/5-day
pattern matches Issurin's 30±5 / 30±5 / 5±3 figures because it is this table:
week1-lecture.md (marker p.66) reproduces Table 1.6 directly, under a slide block that names
"Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source (marker p.64), and gives strength endurance as
~12 days against Issurin's 15±5, the one value where the course departs from the book.

**When NOT to apply** — Treat the numbers as a synthesized rule of thumb
(±5, ±4, ±5, ±3 day spreads are themselves wide relative to the means), not a precise
per-athlete clock; Issurin does not report the sample or method behind Issurin & Lustig
(2004) in this text, so the table's evidentiary base cannot be checked further from this
source alone. Issurin's own surrounding text also notes limits on how far residual-effect
thinking travels: maximum oxygen uptake in highly trained endurance athletes falls when
weekly training volume drops below a certain level (Steinacker, 1993; Steinacker et al.,

aerobic endurance during a taper (Mujika, 1999) (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23).

# Residual Training Effects Last Different Numbers of Days for Different Motor Abilities

**What it is** — The residual training effect is defined as "the retention of changes
induced by systematic workloads beyond a certain time period after the cessation of
training," a term Issurin attributes to Brian and James Counsilman (1991) (PDF p. 33,
printed p. 22). Issurin & Lustig (2004) is cited as the source of Table 1.6 (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), giving residual duration ± SD in days after cessation of training for each
motor ability: **aerobic endurance 30 ± 5 days**, **maximum strength 30 ± 5 days**,
**anaerobic glycolytic endurance 18 ± 4 days**, **strength endurance 15 ± 5 days**,
**maximum speed (alactic) 5 ± 3 days**. Table 1.6's own physiological-background column
lists aerobic endurance's residual as resting on increased aerobic enzymes, mitochondria,
muscle capillaries, hemoglobin capacity, glycogen storage, and fat-metabolism rate, and
maximum strength's on improved neural mechanism and muscle hypertrophy from fiber
enlargement, with no percentages attached in the table itself. Later in the text (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), Issurin gives a specific figure for one of those table items: aerobic
enzymes increase by 40-90% with training (Volkov, 1986; Fox et al., 1993; Wilmore & Costill,
1993). He contrasts this with much smaller local adaptations from sprint training:
phosphocreatine storage (+2-5%), peak lactate accumulation (+10-20%), and anaerobic enzymes
(+2-20%), given without a citation on that page. On the following page (PDF p. 36, printed
p. 25), Thorstensson (1988) is cited specifically for "relatively small increases" in
quickly available energy sources, ATP and phosphocreatine, and enzymes such as creatine
kinase, from highly concentrated sprint training.

**Why it works** — Issurin states the mechanism directly (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp. 24-25):
aerobic ability, supported by pronounced morphological and biochemical changes, is retained
"for a number of weeks at near-peak level," while anaerobic abilities, particularly maximum
sprint speed, "retain near-peak levels for much shorter periods" because peak speed's gains
are smaller and rest on "very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions, which
are relatively unstable and cannot be maintained at the highest level without specially
organized training." Maximum strength's comparably long residual is attributed to pronounced
morphological, biochemical, and neural changes: enlargement of muscle-fiber cross-sectional
area, hyperplasia, recruitment of previously inactive motor units, synchronization of their
activity, and increased motor-neuron discharge frequency (Zatsiorsky, 1995). Strength
endurance's residual is stated to depend on event duration and the degree of
anaerobic-resource mobilization; longer-duration strength endurance has a relatively longer
residual thanks to aerobic adaptation.

**When to apply** — Sequencing which ability to develop first in a training stage (see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]). **Inference:** an ability
with a long residual (aerobic endurance, max strength, 30 ± 5 d) can be built early and
carried further without direct work than a short-residual one, but a stage longer than about
30 days after accumulation ends needs a retention dose (see Example); max speed (5 ± 3 d)
needs re-exposure close to competition. **Eric's baseline directly echoes half of this table:** "Training
residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need
re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue
readiness for max-velocity work degrades" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` p.27). This 30/30/5-day
pattern matches Issurin's 30±5 / 30±5 / 5±3 figures because it is this table:
week1-lecture.md (marker p.66) reproduces Table 1.6 directly, under a slide block that names
"Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source (marker p.64), and gives strength endurance as
~12 days against Issurin's 15±5, the one value where the course departs from the book.

**When NOT to apply** — Treat the numbers as a synthesized rule of thumb
(±5, ±4, ±5, ±3 day spreads are themselves wide relative to the means), not a precise
per-athlete clock; Issurin does not report the sample or method behind Issurin & Lustig
(2004) in this text, so the table's evidentiary base cannot be checked further from this
source alone. Issurin's own surrounding text also notes limits on how far residual-effect
thinking travels: maximum oxygen uptake in highly trained endurance athletes falls when
weekly training volume drops below a certain level (Steinacker, 1993; Steinacker et al.,
1998), and large volumes of highly intense exercise do not prevent detraining and loss of
aerobic endurance during a taper (Mujika, 1999) (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23).

# Immediate, Delayed, and Cumulative Training Effects

**What it is** — A training program produces effects on three timescales: **Immediate** — the acute physiological reaction during and right after a session (↑heart rate, ↑blood pressure, ↓force from fatigue, glycogen depletion). **Delayed** — the lasting positive benefit that appears only *after* the session's fatigue dissipates; the more intense the bout, the longer until the gain is realized. **Cumulative** — the compounding result of many sessions or phases, including threshold-breaking blocks, which can produce a surprising jump in performance ("we worked hard and suddenly it just happened").

**Why it works** — Each session leaves a short-lived acute disturbance and a longer-lived adaptive residue. Good planning — alternating high loads with compensation sessions — lets delayed effects surface and lets residues stack into the cumulative effect. The overall outcome is shaped by current training state, prior bouts, and the order/spacing of all stimuli.

**When to apply** — Setting expectations for *when* gains appear; reassuring during a hard block that suppressed performance is the immediate effect masking a delayed gain; explaining peaking, where a cumulative effect is unmasked by reduced load.

**When NOT to apply** — Don't judge a program by immediate-effect readings alone (a fatigued, depressed test mid-block is expected, not failure). The cumulative effect requires deliberate alternation of load and recovery — pile on intensity without compensation and you get overtraining, not a rebound. See [[heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]] and [[principle--supercompensation-cycle]].

**Example** — An athlete's vertical jump dips through a heavy three-week block (immediate effect), then rebounds above baseline during a deload as the delayed and cumulative effects surface.

# Review: Supertraining section 4.1 (printed 201-206, PDF 212-217), round 1

Reviewer: Claude Opus (independent, instructed to falsify). Date: 2026-09-27.
Scope: the 6 files in `staging/_scope_supertraining_ch4-1.txt`. 4.2 files in the same folder were ignored.
Source: `staging/books/supertraining-6th-expanded.pdf`, PDF pages 212-217 (0-based), text extracted with PyMuPDF and checked against rendered page images for Figure 4.1 (PDF 214) and for every cited author name (PDF 213, 214, 217).

Name spellings as printed (page images, not OCR): "Chernyavsky, 1966" twice at printed 202; "Chenyavsky, 1966" at printed 203; "Khvilon, 1974" and "Khrolon, 1974" both at printed 203; "Nyeniskin, 1974" at 202; "Khodykin" at 206 (the OCR layer reads "Khodvkin"; the image reads Khodykin, so entry 6 is right).

## Entry table

| File | Verdict | Problem (entry vs source, with page) | Exact correction |
|---|---|---|---|
| claim--strength-and-speed-training-response-shifts-with-training-age.md | FIX | (1) Title: "...How to Split Light and Heavy Work, Both Shift With Training Age". The Chernyavsky result is not a training-age finding. The book introduces it with "The magnitude of strength increase and its specific character are also determined by the combination of the training means used" (PDF 213 / p.202); nothing about training age. The body says "Separately", the title does not. (2) When to apply: "(this data uses roughly 16-20 sessions as the shift point)". 16 is Zimkin's session count; 20 is the length of Chernyavsky's study, not a shift point. Also "(per Chernyavsky) a composition weighted toward the heavier... in the first weeks of a new strength block" ties Chernyavsky to early training, which the book does not. (3) "The same passage repeats, from the same Verkhoshansky 1977 source, the Korobkov/Gerasimov/Vasiliev finding": no Verkhoshansky 1977 citation appears in the printed-202 passage (it cites only Korobkov 1953, Gerasimov 1953, Vasiliev 1954). (4) Why it works: "The authors give no mechanism for why the optimal percentage shifts with training age." The book's next paragraph opens "To interpret these factors, one must bear in mind the phasic nature of the response to intense strength loads, characterised by a temporary decrease in strength and speed of movement, and the subsequent increase in strength and speed after the intensity of the resistance has decreased" (PDF 213 / p.202). That is the authors' interpretation of the Zimkin and Muller & Hettinger data. The book also states "the lower the trainee's level of strength, the greater its increase with training. Virtually all training means prove to be beneficial in this case. However, with increase in proficiency, the rate of strength increase diminishes and can be elicited only through sufficiently demanding special means" (PDF 213-214 / pp.202-203), which directly supports the training-age claim and is not captured. | Retitle, e.g. "The Most Effective Training Load Percentage Shifts With Training Age, and the Mix of Light and Heavy Loads Changes Both Strength and Speed Gains". Delete "(this data uses roughly 16-20 sessions as the shift point)" and write "Zimkin's reversal appeared by 16 sessions; Chernyavsky's study ran 20 sessions and is about load mix, not training age". Remove "(per Chernyavsky)" from the early-block sentence. Replace "from the same Verkhoshansky 1977 source" with "(Korobkov 1953; Gerasimov 1953; Vasiliev 1954, printed 202)". Rewrite Why it works: first give the authors' phasic-response interpretation (quote, PDF 213 / p.202) and their "lower the level, greater the increase; virtually all means beneficial" statement (PDF 213-214 / pp.202-203) as plain text; keep the neuromuscular reasoning only as "Inference:". Checked and correct: Zimkin 1961, weightlifters, 45-60% vs 60-75%/75-90% over first 8 sessions, reversal after 16; Muller & Hettinger 1957, 30-46% novices, at least 60% experienced; Chernyavsky 1966, 20 sessions, 20%/80% split, 44.8%/35.2% vs 31.6%/18.3%, all at PDF 213 / p.202. |
| claim--delayed-strength-training-effect-lag-before-gains-appear.md | FIX | (1) Why it works: "The authors themselves hedge the mechanism ('it may be assumed'); no firm explanation is given." The hedge applies only to the Nyeniskin sentence. For the delay itself the book gives a stated interpretation immediately before the Clarke citation: "the phasic nature of the response to intense strength loads, characterised by a temporary decrease in strength and speed of movement, and the subsequent increase in strength and speed after the intensity of the resistance has decreased. Therefore, the effectiveness of heavy weights does not occur immediately, but some time later" (PDF 213 / p.202). The entry omits the book's own mechanism. (2) When NOT to apply: "the 10-day figure comes from one uncontrolled study". The book says nothing about controls: "An increase averaging 18-25% in speed-strength for a controlled movement was noted after a 10 day rest from intense specialised strength training (Nyeniskin, 1974)" (PDF 213 / p.202). "Uncontrolled" is invented (and risks confusion with the book's "controlled movement"). | Add to What it is / Why it works as plain text: the phasic-response statement and "Therefore, the effectiveness of heavy weights does not occur immediately, but some time later" (PDF 213 / p.202). Keep the "it may be assumed" hedge scoped to the Nyeniskin finding only. Replace "comes from one uncontrolled study" with "comes from one study whose design is not described in this text". Add Related link to [[periodization--bompa/framework--three-training-effects]] (delayed training effect, same idea from Bompa). Checked and correct: Clarke 1954 isometric, Chernyavsky 1966 at least 20 sessions, Nyeniskin 1974 18-25%, 10-day rest, "controlled movement", quoted "may be assumed... adaptive inertia... supercompensatory restoration (adaptive reconstruction)" all at PDF 213 / p.202. |
| claim--strength-detraining-and-retention-timelines.md | FIX | (1) Locator: "(PDF pp. 213-214, printed pp. 202-203.)" Every figure in the entry is on PDF 214 / printed 203; nothing comes from 213. (2) "skiers' knee extensor strength dropped 5-6% and flexor strength 15-20%". The book: "the strength of the extensor muscles decreases by 5-6% and the flexors by 15-20% in skiers" (PDF 214 / p.203). No joint is named; "knee" is invented. (3) Contested record: the entry says the authors present both sides "without reconciling" and the title says "the Book Does Not Reconcile Them". True, but the book explicitly acknowledges the conflict: "Although the above findings give an idea of the general tendencies for the increase and maintenance of muscular strength, there are obvious contradictions" (PDF 214 / p.203). The entry should quote that, so it does not read as a contradiction the authors missed. Both sides themselves are recorded correctly (Chernyavsky 20 sessions, 88.8% lost by month 5; Vasiliev 1954 and McMorris & Eklins 1954, 40 sessions, not back to initial levels after a year). (4) Printed spelling: the book prints "Chenyavsky, 1966" here (image, p.203); the entry silently normalizes it to Chernyavsky while noting "Khrolon". (5) When to apply: "for an athlete facing an enforced 1-2 week break... expect... (this text's range: roughly 5-30% depending on tissue and duration)". The 5-6%/15-20% figures are for "1-2 months without systematic strength work"; 30% is for one week of total bed rest (PDF 214 / p.203). Mapping 5-30% onto a 1-2 week ordinary break misapplies both numbers. (6) Why it works Inference: explains Chernyavsky's faster decay by the "shorter, speed-strength-focused 20-session block". The book's own next sentence cuts against a session-count explanation: "A significant proportion of the increase in strength achieved as a result of ten electrostimulation sessions was maintained for 5 months (Khvilon, 1974)" (PDF 214 / p.203). (7) When NOT to apply: "the text's own 40-session data contradicts it for longer training blocks" states block length as the cause, unlabelled; the book gives no cause. (8) The book's own prescription in the same paragraph is missing: "some of the training intensity should be directed at preserving the level of strength attained, which is preferable to restoring strength after it has diminished markedly" (PDF 214 / p.203). | Change locator to "(PDF p. 214, printed p. 203.)". Replace "knee extensor strength" with "extensor muscle strength" and "flexor strength" stays. Add after the contradiction paragraph: 'The authors acknowledge the conflict: "there are obvious contradictions" (PDF 214 / p.203), and call for research on the training effect of means and their optimum sequence, but do not resolve it.' Retitle to "...and the Book Flags but Does Not Resolve the Contradiction". Add "(printed as 'Chenyavsky' in this passage)" after the Chernyavsky decay citation. In When to apply, replace the bracket with: "(Inference: this text gives no figure for a 1-2 week ordinary break; its nearest figures are 5-6% extensor and 15-20% flexor loss after 1-2 months, and up to 30% after one week of total bed rest, a more severe condition)". In Why it works, add: "Inference, with a caveat: the book's own Khvilon (1974) data, 10 electrostimulation sessions with much of the gain kept for 5 months, do not fit a simple session-count explanation." In When NOT, change to "Inference: block length may explain the difference, but the book does not say so; its 40-session data contradict the 20-session decay curve." Add as plain text in When to apply: the authors' preserve-rather-than-restore prescription with the quote and page. Add Related: [[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]] (max strength 30 +/- 5 days, the source behind Eric's baseline 30-day line) and [[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--three-types-of-overload-stimulating-retaining-detraining]]. Checked and correct: Muller 1966 up to 30% after 1 week bed rest; Hettinger & Muller 1955 and Ravick & Larsen 1959 same-rate loss; uncited 7-10 day layoff soreness; Chernyavsky 8.8/33.8/60.2/81.5/88.8%, greatest loss months 2-4; Vasiliev 1954 and McMorris & Eklins 1954, 40 sessions, a year; Khvilon 1974, 10 electrostimulation sessions, 5 months; DeLorme 1950 and "Khrolon" 1974 on muscle mass (all PDF 214 / p.203). Eric's baseline quote verified at `method-baseline.md` line 150, "Periodization and programming", citing class1 transcript p.27. `contested` is justified by the book's own stated contradiction. |
| framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order.md | GO | No blocking problem. The algebraic framing is the book's: heading "Algebraic Relations and Training" and "Two algebraic laws may be applied to the interaction between different means, methods and techniques in strength (and all sports) training, which are important because they are not generally obeyed in training" (PDF 216 / p.205). Optional nits for the fixer: (a) When to apply paraphrases "Virtually any training may be rendered impotent or harmful if it is administered in an inappropriate manner for a given individual [at a] given stage" (PDF 217 / p.206) as "through an inappropriate combination or timing"; closer wording would be "administered in an inappropriate manner". (b) The book extends non-commutativity to "successive microcycles or mesocycles in a periodised program" and to complex-training methods (PDF 216 / p.205); the entry only gestures at this in Why it works; one sentence in What it is would help. (c) Add Related: [[framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing]] (the book's own after-effect sequencing data). | None required. Checked: Commutative A*B = B*A and Associative A*(B*C) = (A*B)*C stated as not generally obeyed (PDF 216 / p.205); squat/clean order example; "a distance running session shortly before a weights session will invariably decrease one's strength capabilities" (quote exact); muscle endurance A, plyometrics B, Olympic lifting C associative example (all PDF 216 / p.205); hybrid exercises Ch 7.1 (PDF 216); after-effect sentence "exercises in different parts of a workout, on different training days and even separated by several days or weeks can interact positively or negatively" (PDF 216 / p.205); the quoted remarks "power cleans are useless", "periodisation doesn't work", "circuit training is excellent for general preparation" (PDF 216-217 / pp.205-206). Why it works mechanism correctly labelled Inference; When NOT labelled Inference; Example uses only the book's own examples. Locator PDF 216-217 / 205-206 correct. No vault duplicate ("commutative" appears nowhere else as a concept). |
| framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy.md | FIX | (1) When to apply, second sentence: "Use the particular/cumulative distinction to judge whether a training block's variety is producing an integrated adaptation or just a list of separate, unintegrated stimuli, and use the five generalizations as a checklist" is the writer's application, unlabelled. (The first sentence, rest interval lengthened or shortened by the ATE, is the book's, PDF 215 / p.204.) (2) Example: "pairing a heavy back squat (a depleting ATE) immediately before max-velocity sprint work would likely blunt that day's sprint quality... avoids that particular-effect interference."
